lessons.title: Greedy Strategy Fundamentals
lessons.concept: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step by choosing the option that looks best at the current moment (locally optimal choice), hoping this leads to a globally optimal solution. Greedy methods are efficient but correct only for problems with suitable properties.
lessons.formula: Greedy choice: pick best local option now + reduce problem. Correctness often needs greedy-choice property and optimal substructure (problem-dependent).
lessons.worked_example: Coin change with denominations [1,2,5,10] for amount 18: repeatedly pick largest coin <= remaining (10,5,2,1) gives 4 coins. This works for canonical coin systems but not for all arbitrary denominations.
mistakes: Assuming greedy always yields optimal solution for every problem
Not proving or recognizing when local choice is safe

lessons.title: Common Greedy Patterns
lessons.concept: Typical greedy patterns include activity/interval selection (choose earliest finishing compatible activity), fractional knapsack (take highest value/weight ratio first), minimum platforms/resources by sorting events, and Huffman-like merging (conceptually). Sorting is often a preprocessing step.
lessons.formula: Pattern examples: interval scheduling -> sort by finish time, pick non-overlapping. Fractional knapsack -> sort by value/weight desc, take as much as possible.
lessons.worked_example: Activities with (start,end): (1,3),(2,5),(4,6). Sort by end: (1,3),(4,6),(2,5). Pick (1,3), skip (2,5) (overlaps), pick (4,6). Max non-overlapping = 2.
mistakes: Sorting by the wrong key (e.g., start time instead of finish time for activity selection)
Applying fractional knapsack logic to 0/1 knapsack
Ignoring feasibility constraints after making a greedy choice

lessons.title: When Greedy Works and When It Fails
lessons.concept: Greedy algorithms work when a locally optimal choice can be part of some globally optimal solution and the problem has optimal substructure. They fail when early choices block better overall combinations; in such cases, dynamic programming or exhaustive search may be required.
lessons.formula: Check: greedy-choice property + optimal substructure. Counterexample testing is useful to detect failure cases.
lessons.worked_example: 0/1 knapsack with items (w,v): (10,60),(20,100),(30,120), capacity 50. Greedy by ratio picks (10,60) and (20,100) value 160, but optimal is (20,100)+(30,120) value 220. Greedy fails here.
mistakes: Not testing counterexamples for a proposed greedy rule
Believing a few correct examples prove correctness
Using greedy for 0/1 knapsack instead of DP/backtracking as appropriate
